text: A pig farmer is told, in a vision, that he is Magloire the First, prophet of Christ. Roger Gnoan M'Bala plays it straight for eighty minutes, which is the sharper choice, because the joke was never the vision. It is everything that has to happen next: a prophet needs a village willing to be saved, and this one already has its own arrangements with the invisible. Magloire's campaign against the old rites runs into neighbours who have been managing without him. The film watches a man with no authority except conviction acquire some anyway, and it spares neither side of the quarrel. Comedy at this length cannot dawdle; the rise has to be quick, and the quicker it is the more it exposes. Made in Côte d'Ivoire, in French, with pigs in the yard and scripture in the mouth.

In Brussels, a king from Congo goes looking for his daughter, and the city has no machinery for registering that he is a king. Mwezé Ngangura is less interested in the search than in what the search requires: the asking, the waiting, the explaining of oneself to strangers with no reason to listen twice. The story crosses a continent, but the film spends itself in rooms rather than on distances. French does the carrying, the language both ends of the journey happen to share. The premise could have been played for pathos. Instead the man's composure becomes the method, and the pressure falls on everyone who has to decide how to address him, which is a decision about themselves, made quickly, in front of him.

Benjamin is thirteen and has never met his father; when his mother goes to prison, that is where he is sent. The father turns out to be a warehouseman in his mid-forties who still lives with his Moroccan parents in a high-rise in the banlieue, so the boy arrives not into a rescue but into a flat where three generations are already stepping around one another. Hicham Ayouch does not soften the child to make him easier to hold. Benjamin has been moved between care homes since he was small, and difficulty is the one possession he has managed to keep. What the film measures is patience: how much a household barely coping keeps in reserve, and how fast a thirteen-year-old can spend it. The pressure never eases: too many people, one flat, a boy nobody in it chose.

Two women share a consulting room, and only one of them is supposed to be the patient. Rihana arrives pregnant and traumatised, raised as a son by a father who permitted no other version of her; Zineb, the psychiatrist assigned to the case, has material of her own that the sessions start to disturb. Mohamed Mouftakir builds the film on that leak between them. The professional frame of appointments and questions and notes is precisely what the story takes apart, slowly, and in Arabic. A father who decides what his daughter is permitted to be is not a figure of speech here; he is a household arrangement whose terms are still binding on the grown woman in the chair. The film's question is who the damage belongs to once it has been said out loud.

Thirty-five minutes, Niger, 1970: a man comes home from Mecca with the title el hadji and a wish to marry a third time. Oumarou Ganda gives the situation no cushioning at all. The woman he wants, Santou, is his daughter's friend and is already promised to Garba; the house he would bring her into already holds two wives, the second of whom, Gaika, can calculate exactly what a younger arrival subtracts from her. At this length nothing can be developed, only arranged, and the arrangement is the argument, with devotion and appetite walking through the same door on the same afternoon. The film carries the Étalon d'Or de Yennenga. What stays is that the women are given reasoning rather than reaction: each can say what the household costs and what she is owed.

A carpet is the object everyone sees; this film stays upstream of it, among the dye, the wool packs, and the backs that carry them. An old dyer and his son Miloud do the hauling, and Souheil Ben-Barka keeps the arithmetic visible: one finished piece, thousands of hands, almost none of which will be named beside it. Sixty minutes, in French, out of Morocco in 1972. Children are part of that workforce, and the boy at the centre is not there to be adorable; he is there because his hands are in the total. The film moves less like a story than like a tally, gathering weight through repetition, the same tasks and rooms and the same wool advanced one stage further. Ben-Barka is not indignant on the viewer's behalf. He keeps the camera where the work is, which turns out to be enough.

Quincy Bosomfield is a district commissioner, which means he administers his own people on behalf of the men who educated him. Kwaw Ansah made the film in Ghana in 1989 and made it in English, the language of that education and of the desk it earned. The interest is not in hypocrisy, which would be easy and short. It is in the accounting: what a man surrenders in exchange for a title, and the way the surrender is asked for in small instalments, each reasonable at the time. A hundred and ten minutes gives that erosion room to happen at something close to its real speed. Nobody has to be a villain for this to work, and the men who trained Bosomfield never need to raise their voices. The film takes him seriously enough to show what he thought he was buying.

Kramoko is the son of a griot; Fanta is of noble blood; in the world they live in, that is the entire obstacle. Fadika Kramo-Lanciné, filming in Côte d'Ivoire in 1981, refuses to let the prohibition stand as nature. The film goes back to find where the rule began, which is a decision with consequences: once a custom has an origin it also has authors, and the couple's manoeuvres stop looking like impatience. The weight sits less on the lovers, whose feelings are settled early, than on the households that would absorb the breach — a griot's standing, a family's name, neighbours with opinions and long memories. The tone is not grievance. It is closer to a patient argument made in front of people who have heard it before, and who will decide.

A man kills the king at his wife's urging and takes the throne, and the film begins there instead of ending there. What Dani Kouyaté is after is the maintenance: a crown held by someone who knows precisely how it was obtained and therefore knows every way it can be taken back. The wife is not a spectator to the plan, and the plan does not end once the throne is occupied — keeping it requires a second act of the same kind, then a third, each cheaper than the last. It comes from Burkina Faso, in Fulah, and carries the Stallion of Yennenga. Films about power often ask for admiration on the way up. This one is more interested in the days after, when everyone who helped is still alive, still nearby, and still owed something.

The children do the deciding: they find the donor themselves, without telling either of their mothers. By the time Nic and Jules learn of it, a stranger is standing inside an arrangement two decades in the making, and he is being pleasant about it. Lisa Cholodenko keeps the film in comedy for as long as comedy will hold, which is longer than expected, because everyone behaves well at first and good behaviour is where the damage hides. Whether two women can raise a family is not the question; that was settled before the first scene. The attention goes instead to the ordinary friction of a long marriage conducted with witnesses in the house. The tone shifts underneath without announcing itself. Sympathy moves more than once, and nobody has to behave badly for it to move.

Twenty-four thousand dollars, given away in 1992 by a graduate who then started moving north. Sean Penn takes two and a half hours to deliver Christopher McCandless to Alaska, and the length is the argument: the wilderness is the destination, but the film is mostly road, mostly other people, mostly the slow work of shedding a life that by every visible measure was going well. A degree from Emory, a record as a top student and athlete, a savings account — handed over early, all of it. What replaces them has to be earned scene by scene, and the strangers met along the way are allowed to answer back rather than serve as scenery. Penn films the refusal as a decision taken by someone capable, which is more unsettling than filming it as a breakdown. The pull of it is that the reasoning almost holds.

A playwright who cannot start his next thing begins spending his afternoons with a widow and her four sons. The film knows that needs accounting for, and Marc Forster's answer is to show the work rather than assert the inspiration: J.M. Barrie is not collecting material so much as finding the only company that lets a grown man play without looking foolish. The theatre carries the professional weight, a writer with nothing to deliver, while the household scenes stay at child height, which is where the invention actually occurs. The picture is courteous with its time; nothing is hurried and nothing is laboured. Peter Pan comes out of this, and the film takes care to make its arrival look like a run of small accidents rather than a destiny.

A policeman stops taking the money, and the danger that follows comes not from criminals but from the men sitting beside him in the car. Sidney Lumet builds Serpico by accumulation rather than crisis: a refusal, then another refusal, then the discovery that there is no office in the building where what he knows can safely be left. The film is history as much as crime, and the classification is honest — this is procedure, not caper, and its suspense is administrative. What it costs Frank Serpico is measured in ordinary units: who will partner him, who answers when he calls for help, who stands near him at the end of a shift. There is very little relief anywhere in it. The screenplay took the WGA award for adaptation, and the discipline shows in how seldom anyone makes a speech.

New York, the winter of 1981, statistically among the most violent years in the city's own records — and the story picked out of it is a man trying to grow a business. J.C. Chandor keeps the violence at the edge of the frame, where it behaves like weather: something the family plans around, budgets for, and declines to discuss. The National Board of Review named it the year's best film, which for a picture this reluctant about its own genre is a fair reading. The immigrant at the centre has built something and wants it larger, and every route to larger runs past someone who expects a share. His family is inside the enterprise, not waiting at home for news of it. The pace is deliberate and most of it is negotiation. The suspense is contractual, and it holds.
